judge_refusal_prior_art.paper: GuidedBench: Measuring and Mitigating the Evaluation Discrepancies of In-the-wild LLM Jailbreak Methods
judge_refusal_prior_art.what_measured: Inter-evaluator variance of scoring across LLM-as-judge systems on ~20,000 jailbreak cases, plus a design decision (evaluator selection) intended to avoid grader refusal on harmful content. Judges: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), DeepSeek-V3, Doubao-v1.5-pro. Reports variance reduction, NOT a grader refusal/degeneracy rate.
judge_refusal_prior_art.judges: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Doubao-v1.5-pro (all selected as 'less safety-restricted' specifically to avoid triggering refusals during grading; GPT-3.5 explicitly excluded because its 'strict safety filters ... often trigger refusals on harmful inputs during evaluation, resulting in missing data')
judge_refusal_prior_art.number: GuidedEval reduces inter-evaluator score variance by 76.03% to 88.28% versus baseline LLM-as-judge systems (Table 6). No refusal-rate percentage is printed anywhere in the paper.
judge_refusal_prior_art.locator: Abstract; Section 5.2 'Mitigating Disagreement of Judge Models', page 9 (page marker '8' precedes this text block, 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026' page-9 header follows it)
judge_refusal_prior_art.quote: This indicates that GuidedEval significantly reduces its dependency on LLM evaluators, enabling users to select evaluator APIs with stronger context extraction and reasoning capabilities yet less restrictive in safety constraints, thus ensuring evaluators do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content.

judge_refusal_prior_art.paper: An Empirical Measurement of Jailbreaking Evaluators
judge_refusal_prior_art.what_measured: Agreement of six automated jailbreak evaluators (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, JailbreakRadar, StrongReject, JADES, JailMeter) with human labels on two human-labeled datasets (JailbreakQR, JailMeter-Eva); reports accuracy, precision, recall, F1, FPR per evaluator. Does NOT discuss or quantify evaluator/grader-side refusal-to-grade or degenerate (e.g. all-ones) output; that phenomenon is absent from the paper (checked via regex for 'judge refus', 'declin', 'error type').
judge_refusal_prior_art.judges: Shared LLM judge backbone fixed across the 5 evaluators that need one (paper does not name the specific backbone model in the excerpted text; StrongReject uses its own released refusal-gate + rubric)
judge_refusal_prior_art.number: On JailbreakQR: StrongReject 89.5% accuracy / 89.8% F1 / 87.6% recall / 8.4% FPR vs human labels; JADES 92.3% accuracy / 92.5% F1 / 5.8% FPR (best); HarmBench 88.3% accuracy / 88.5% F1; JailbreakBench lowest F1 at 81.2%.
judge_refusal_prior_art.quote: On JailbreakQR, it reaches 92.3% accuracy and 92.5% F1, while also producing the lowest false positive rate at 5.8%. StrongReject follows with 89.5% accuracy and 89.8% F1, while HarmBench also performs consistently well with 88.3% accuracy and 88.5% F1.

judge_refusal_prior_art.paper: JAILJUDGE: A Comprehensive Jailbreak Judge Benchmark with Multi-Agent Enhanced Explanation Evaluation Framework
judge_refusal_prior_art.what_measured: Judge-vs-human disagreement (F1) of a GPT-4 LLM-as-judge on complex/OOD jailbreak-judgment scenarios; motivates a multi-agent judge framework. This is an accuracy/disagreement number, not a refusal-to-grade rate.
judge_refusal_prior_art.number: F1 score of the GPT-4 judge is only 55% in complex scenarios.
judge_refusal_prior_art.quote: Current evaluation methods lack explainability and do not generalize well to complex scenarios, resulting in incomplete and inaccurate assessments (e.g., direct judgment without reasoning explainability, the F1 score of the GPT-4 judge is only 55% in complex scenarios and bias evaluation on multilingual scenarios, etc.).

judge_refusal_prior_art.paper: AdvPrefix: An Objective for Nuanced LLM Jailbreaks
judge_refusal_prior_art.what_measured: Judge-refinement study: the original naive judge sometimes fails on sensitive completions, so the authors add 'affirmative prefilling to handle sensitive content' to a revised Llama-3.1-70B judge and report the resulting improvement in human-agreement rate. No isolated refusal-rate percentage is printed for the judge itself (the 9% figure bundles three simultaneous fixes: reasoning traces, completeness/faithfulness instructions, and affirmative prefilling).
judge_refusal_prior_art.judges: Llama-3.1-70B (revised judge, using affirmative prefilling + reasoning-trace instructions)
judge_refusal_prior_art.number: Revised judge improves human agreement rates by up to 9% on newer LLMs (conflated across 3 simultaneous fixes, not isolated to the prefilling/refusal fix).
judge_refusal_prior_art.quote: we develop a refined judge using Llama-3.1-70B, with revised instructions prioritizing response completeness and faithfulness, requiring reasoning traces before giving the final answer, and affirmative prefilling to handle sensitive content ... This judge improves human agreement rates by up to 9% on newer LLMs.

judge_refusal_prior_art.what_measured: Checked whether the original StrongREJECT paper itself discusses or quantifies grader-side refusal-to-evaluate. It does not: the paper's use of 'refuse' is entirely about the VICTIM model refusing the harmful prompt (defining jailbreak success/failure), never about the grading LLM refusing to score a response.
judge_refusal_prior_art.judges: n/a (paper discusses its own rubric/judge design but not judge refusal)
judge_refusal_prior_art.number: NOT_FOUND -- no evaluator/grader refusal number is printed anywhere in the paper (regex-checked for judge-refusal phrasing, degenerate-output phrasing, and literal '1,1,1').
judge_refusal_prior_art.quote: the most significant oversight of past automated evaluation methods is their over-emphasis ... on non-refusal, defining a jailbreak as 'successful' merely if the victim model's response does not explicitly refuse to answer the jailbroken prompt

guidedbench_verdict.claimed_phrase: GuidedEval is designed so that judges 'do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content'
guidedbench_verdict.actual_quote: This indicates that GuidedEval significantly reduces its dependency on LLM evaluators, enabling users to select evaluator APIs with stronger context extraction and reasoning capabilities yet less restrictive in safety constraints, thus ensuring evaluators do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content. Hence, GuidedEval helps reduce the overall cost of conducting scalable and reliable jailbreak evaluations.
guidedbench_verdict.locator: Section 5.2 'Mitigating Disagreement of Judge Models', page 9
guidedbench_verdict.caveat: The phrase exists essentially as the reviewer described, but it describes a DESIGN CHOICE (picking less-safety-restricted evaluator backbones: GPT-4o / DeepSeek-V3 / Doubao-v1.5-pro, explicitly excluding GPT-3.5 because its safety filters trigger refusals) plus the headline empirical result is inter-evaluator VARIANCE reduction (76.03%-88.28%, Table 6), not a measured judge-refusal RATE. GuidedBench does not report how often any judge actually refused/degenerated before or after this design choice, and it uses different judges (GPT-4o/DeepSeek-V3/Doubao) than our gpt-5-mini/gemini-2.5-flash. So the reviewer's underlying point (this failure mode is known) is correct and directly supported; what GuidedBench does NOT do is quantify grader refusal/degeneracy rate per judge x framing the way our calibration-set adjudication does.

positioning_grader_refusal: That LLM judges sometimes refuse, or degenerate into a uniform score, when grading responses to harmful prompts under a StrongREJECT-style rubric \citep{Souly2024} is not a new observation: \citet{Huang2025} deliberately select less safety-restricted evaluator backbones so that they "do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content," and \citet{Zhu2024} add affirmative prefilling to their judge prompt because the underlying model otherwise declines to grade sensitive completions. What is new here is not the existence of grader-side refusal but its quantification: for two judges (gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash) crossed with each rubric framing, we measure how often the grader itself refuses or degenerates, directly on a 60 known-compliant + 60 known-refusal calibration set where the ground-truth label is fixed in advance. We do not claim that published StrongREJECT evaluations overestimated safety; a literal all-ones (1,1,1) rubric output is also the rubric's correct, legitimate score for a genuine victim-model refusal, so any headline number must first separate that legitimate case from true grader failure -- which is precisely what our per-judge x framing adjudication contributes.

citation_fixes.wrong_text: OR-Bench and similar suites extend coverage to multi-turn settings [Kaushik2025]
citation_fixes.problem: Kaushik2025 in references.bib (arXiv 2512.05117) is 'The Universal Weight Subspace Hypothesis' by Prakhar Kaushik, Shravan Chaudhari, Ankit Vaidya, Rama Chellappa, Alan Yuille -- an unrelated weight-space/subspace paper with no connection to over-refusal benchmarks, jailbreak evaluation, or multi-turn conversation. The citation is fabricated/misattributed. Separately, OR-Bench itself (Cui2024, arXiv 2405.20947) is a SINGLE-TURN prompt benchmark (80,000 over-refusal prompts, ~1,000 hard prompts, 600 toxic prompts across 10 rejection categories, evaluated on 32 LLMs); its abstract makes no multi-turn claim.
citation_fixes.corrected_text: OR-Bench remains a single-turn benchmark: 80,000 seemingly-toxic prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a 1,000-prompt hard subset, and 600 toxic prompts, evaluated on 32 LLMs across 8 model families \citep{Cui2024}. It does not extend coverage to multi-turn conversational settings, and we drop the Kaushik2025 citation, which names an unrelated weight-subspace paper (arXiv 2512.05117) with no bearing on over-refusal or multi-turn evaluation.
citation_fixes.quote: OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses. We then conduct a comprehensive study to measure the over-refusal of 32 popular LLMs across 8 model families.
citation_fixes.locator: arXiv:2405.20947 abstract; venue: accepted to ICML 2025
citation_fixes.recommendation: REMOVE the Kaushik2025 citation from this sentence entirely; it should not be cited anywhere near over-refusal/multi-turn claims. If a genuine multi-turn over-refusal citation is needed, a new source must be found and verified -- none was substituted here per task instructions (no invented citation).

citation_fixes.wrong_text: Tamirisa et al. (2408.00761) show that weight edits can flip refusal, with a consistent loss plateau across 500 steps and sweeping learning rate, adapter rank and chat-template variants
citation_fixes.problem: TAR (Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs) is exclusively about GRADIENT-BASED FINE-TUNING attacks (SFT with up to 1,000 steps) against a meta-learned tamper-resistance safeguard -- it never performs or claims that TRAINING-FREE, single-shot WEIGHT EDITS (e.g. activation steering, weight orthogonalization/ablation) can flip refusal. The red-teaming grid varies optimizer, number of optimization steps, learning rate, learning rate schedule, fine-tuning dataset, batch size, and fine-tuning method (full vs. parameter-efficient) -- there is zero mention of 'adapter rank' or 'chat template' anywhere in the paper (regex-checked, 0 matches for both terms). The loss-plateau claim is real but is for 500 STEPS OF AN SFT ATTACK on a TAR-protected biosecurity forget-set, not a plateau 'across... adapter rank and chat-template variants.'
citation_fixes.corrected_text: Tamirisa et al. (\citet{Tamirisa2024}) show that their meta-learned tamper-resistance safeguard (TAR) withstands gradient-based fine-tuning attacks (SFT, varying optimizer, learning rate, learning-rate schedule, fine-tuning dataset, batch size and full vs. parameter-efficient fine-tuning) for a consistent loss plateau over 500 of up to 1,000 attack steps. TAR does not test, and its safeguard is not designed against, training-free single-shot weight edits (e.g. activation steering or weight orthogonalization/ablation); we therefore no longer cite it for the claim that weight edits can flip refusal.
citation_fixes.quote: TAR yields a consistent loss plateau for 500 steps, followed by a loss region of increased variability. ... We vary the optimizer, number of optimization steps, learning rate, learning rate schedule, fine-tuning dataset, batch size, and overall fine-tuning method (e.g., full fine-tuning versus parameter-efficient fine-tuning). By default, our attacks use 500 fine-tuning steps.
citation_fixes.locator: arXiv:2408.00761, Figure 5 caption (loss plateau) and Section 5/'Weaponization Knowledge Restriction' red-teaming setup (attack grid)

citation_fixes.wrong_text: (implicit in prior draft) Arditi et al.'s single-direction claim is an oversimplification because our Step-1 result found SafeRL and abliteration occupy different subspaces
citation_fixes.problem: Arditi et al. (2406.11717) support exactly two claims, verified from the abstract: (1) erasing a single found direction from residual-stream activations PREVENTS refusal on harmful instructions (removal claim, underlies abliteration), and (2) ADDING that direction ELICITS refusal even on harmless instructions (induction claim). Both are about a single model's OWN refusal direction found by contrastive activation differences; Arditi never claims that two DIFFERENT interventions (e.g. SafeRL fine-tuning vs. abliteration) must move along the SAME direction. Our Step-1 finding (SHARED_SUBSPACE_DIFFERENT_DIRECTIONS: first principal angle 31.1 deg vs. anisotropy-matched null, mean-shift cosine -0.09 at the null, max |cos| 0.20 vs. null p95 0.41, positive control abliterated-vs-abliterated 0.885 vs. null 0.750) is therefore CONSISTENT with, not a refutation of, Arditi: abliteration removes the refusal direction by construction (that IS Arditi's mechanism), so a differently-trained intervention (SafeRL) landing in the same low-dimensional subspace but along a different direction inside it is the expected pattern, not evidence against a single-direction account. For the multi-direction nuance we instead cite Joad2026 (arXiv 2602.02132, verified title 'There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction', EMNLP 2026), whose abstract explicitly shows refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions that nonetheless act as a 'shared one-dimensional control knob' under linear steering -- directly analogous to our shared-subspace-different-directions finding.
citation_fixes.corrected_text: Arditi et al. show that a single direction, when erased from a model's residual stream, prevents refusal on harmful instructions, and, when added, elicits refusal on harmless ones \citep{Arditi2024}. Our Step-1 result -- SafeRL and abliteration share a low-dimensional subspace (first principal angle 31.1$^\circ$ vs. the anisotropy-matched null) but move along different directions within it (mean-shift cosine -0.09, at the sign-flip null; max $|\cos|$ 0.20 vs. null $p_{95}$ 0.41; positive control, abliterated-vs-abliterated, at 0.885 vs. null 0.750) -- is consistent with, not a refutation of, \citet{Arditi2024}: abliteration removes the refusal direction by construction, so an independently-trained intervention landing in the same subspace along a different direction is expected, not evidence that a single direction is an oversimplification. For the multi-direction view we instead follow \citet{Joad2026}, who show refusal categories occupy geometrically distinct directions that nonetheless behave as a shared linear control knob under steering.
citation_fixes.quote: we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace ... we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions.

arditi_reconciliation.reason_quote: The pre-stated reconciliation hypothesis holds: the edits share a low-dimensional subspace that is *not* just the generic high-variance subspace, while moving along different directions inside it.
arditi_reconciliation.supporting_context: Line 68 of the same file, in the numbers ledger summary: 'iteration 2's step1_anchor says SHARED_SUBSPACE while d1_step1 says DIFFERENT_SUBSPACES; resolved above.' The iter-3 evaluation re-ran the Step-1 module on the iter-2 data, fixed a bug (a first version reported SHARED_ANISOTROPY_ONLY because the post-projection 'first' angle was actually the largest principal angle; a self-check assert angle == acos(first_cos) now runs at every site), and reconciled the two contradictory iter-2 verdicts into SHARED_SUBSPACE_DIFFERENT_DIRECTIONS: the first principal angle between SafeRL and abliteration difference matrices remains significant even after projecting out the top-5 instruct principal components (47.7 deg vs. post-projection null p5 68 deg), while the mean-shift cosines between the two interventions' direction vectors stay at the sign-flip null (|cos| ~0.15-0.22 vs. null p95 ~0.24) -- i.e. shared low-dimensional subspace, but not the same direction inside it.
arditi_reconciliation.verdict_text: SHARED_SUBSPACE_DIFFERENT_DIRECTIONS (iter-3), superseding the internally-inconsistent iter-2 pair of verdicts (step1_anchor.json: SHARED_SUBSPACE; d1_step1.json: DIFFERENT_SUBSPACES). Reproduced numbers: 31.11 deg mean first principal angle (last prompt token), -0.092 mean cosine between mean-difference vectors, max |cos| 0.201 vs. null p95 0.417, positive control (abliterated-vs-abliterated) 0.885 vs. null 0.750 (recomputed; differs from iter-2's cherry-picked 0.92/0.72).

sources.title: GuidedBench: Measuring and Mitigating the Evaluation Discrepancies of In-the-wild LLM Jailbreak Methods
sources.authors: Ruixuan Huang, Xun-Guang Wang, Zongjie Li, Daoyuan Wu, Shuai Wang
sources.summary: Proposes GuidedEval, a guideline-based jailbreak-evaluation system, and shows it reduces inter-evaluator score variance by 76.03%-88.28% vs. keyword and prior LLM-judge baselines (StrongREJECT, PAIR, HarmBench). Judges used: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Doubao-v1.5-pro, deliberately chosen to be less safety-restricted so they do not refuse to grade harmful content; GPT-3.5 explicitly excluded for triggering refusals during grading.

passages.quote: GuidedEval reduces inter-evaluator variance by at least 76.03%, ensuring reliable and reproducible evaluations.

This indicates that GuidedEval significantly reduces its dependency on LLM evaluators, enabling users to select evaluator APIs with stronger context extraction and reasoning capabilities yet less restrictive in safety constraints, thus ensuring evaluators do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content.
strict safety filters (e.g., in GPT-3.5) often trigger refusals on harmful inputs during evaluation, resulting in missing data

sources.title: An Empirical Measurement of Jailbreaking Evaluators
sources.summary: Systematically compares six jailbreak evaluators (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, JailbreakRadar, StrongReject, JADES, JailMeter) against human labels on two human-labeled datasets. JADES performs best; StrongReject and HarmBench also perform well (~88-90% accuracy/F1). Does not discuss or quantify grader/judge-side refusal-to-evaluate.

passages.quote: We systematically compare six evaluators that recur in recent jailbreak attack and defense research: HarmBench, JailbreakBench, JailbreakRadar, StrongReject, JADES, and JailMeter.
On JailbreakQR, it reaches 92.3% accuracy and 92.5% F1 ... StrongReject follows with 89.5% accuracy and 89.8% F1, while HarmBench also performs consistently well with 88.3% accuracy and 88.5% F1.

sources.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
sources.authors: Justin Cui, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ion Stoica, Cho-Jui Hsieh
sources.summary: Single-turn over-refusal benchmark: 80,000 seemingly-toxic prompts across 10 rejection categories, ~1,000 hard prompts, 600 toxic prompts; evaluates over-refusal on 32 LLMs across 8 model families. No multi-turn claim.

passages.quote: OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses.

sources.title: The Universal Weight Subspace Hypothesis
sources.authors: Prakhar Kaushik, Shravan Chaudhari, Ankit Vaidya, Rama Chellappa, Alan Yuille
sources.summary: This is what the bib key Kaushik2025 actually points to: a weight-subspace hypothesis paper unrelated to over-refusal benchmarks or multi-turn evaluation. Confirms the draft's citation for 'multi-turn settings' is misattributed and must be dropped.

sources.title: Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
sources.summary: TAR: a meta-learned safeguard resisting gradient-based fine-tuning attacks (SFT, up to 1,000 steps) that try to recover weaponization knowledge or restore refusal-bypassing behavior in open-weight LLMs. Red-teaming grid varies optimizer, steps, learning rate, LR schedule, dataset, batch size, and full vs. parameter-efficient fine-tuning -- no mention of adapter rank or chat templates, and no training-free weight-edit attacks are tested.

passages.quote: TAR yields a consistent loss plateau for 500 steps, followed by a loss region of increased variability.

We vary the optimizer, number of optimization steps, learning rate, learning rate schedule, fine-tuning dataset, batch size, and overall fine-tuning method (e.g., full fine-tuning versus parameter-efficient fine-tuning). By default, our attacks use 500 fine-tuning steps.

sources.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
sources.authors: Andy Arditi, Oscar Obeso, Aaquib Syed, Daniel Paleka, Nina Panickssery, Wes Gurnee, Neel Nanda
sources.summary: Finds a single direction per model such that erasing it from residual-stream activations removes refusal, while adding it induces refusal even on harmless inputs; proposes a white-box abliteration jailbreak from this.

passages.quote: we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions.

sources.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
sources.authors: Faaiz Joad, Majd Hawasly, Sabri Boughorbel, Nadir Durrani, Husrev Taha Sencar
sources.summary: Shows refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space, yet steering along any of them produces near-identical refusal/over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob -- directly analogous to our SHARED_SUBSPACE_DIFFERENT_DIRECTIONS finding.

passages.quote: across diverse refusal and non-compliance categories, refusal behaviors correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space. Yet activation steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal--over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob.
